items.excerpt: National University of Singapore researchers built AI methods that automatically identify a small set of hidden variables capturing a material's collective behavior, letting them predict very large stochastic systems from simulations of much smaller ones. The work (Physical Review Materials and ICML 2026) sharply cuts the compute needed for materials modeling.

Tohoku University unveiled a closed-loop framework that fuses materials databases, machine-learning interatomic potentials, LLMs, AI agents and automated lab workflows so predictions are continuously refined by real experimental feedback. The team says the self-driving-lab approach could shorten clean-energy materials development by years.

Google Quantum AI developed a machine-learning approach that continuously re-tunes a quantum computer as it runs, reusing error-detection events to stabilize the system and achieving about 3.5x greater stability than existing methods. It could let quantum calculations run far longer without costly interruptions.

Stanford and SLAC researchers built an agentic AI 'X-ray scientist' that autonomously aligns crystal samples at synchrotron beamlines, reasoning about experimental conditions and issuing instrument commands. Published in Nature Machine Intelligence, it points toward self-running beamline experiments.

A study led by Ivan Jaric warns that LLMs are becoming normalized in life-sciences research before clear usage boundaries exist, potentially eroding cross-disciplinary collaboration and core scientific skills. It argues routine reliance could reshape the foundations of scientific practice and culture.

Triplebar Bio, UC Berkeley and BioMADE are developing an AI cell-engineering model built specifically for the biomanufacturing environment to optimize host-cell performance, reduce development timelines and streamline platform design. It targets a data regime that generic protein models miss.
